drafts.title: Massachusetts SMART 3.0 Community Shared Solar: written savings floors for renters.
drafts.window: Friday 1 PM or 3 PM MT (heatmap). Evening 8-11 PM OK as second shot.
drafts.angle: SMART 3.0 makes community shared solar rules sharper for households who cannot put panels on a roof: 900 MW annual cap; facilities 40% low-income OR ≥15% bill credits free to LI; standard subscribers ≥20% savings on credit value; LI ≥40% discount; income self-attestation; bans early termination fees; AOBC tied to basic service (~10.79¢/kWh National Grid large vs retail >34¢); independent developers; up to 5 MW (10 MW brownfield/landfill). Soft-pedal Thu CO+NJ LIVE and Illinois/Maryland/CPS twins. Kitchen-table: ask for the written discount %, not a vague "up to."
bullets: SMART 3.0 program year design includes a 900 MW annual capacity frame and a Community Shared Solar set-aside path.
Community Shared facilities must either reserve about 40% for low-income customers OR deliver at least 15% of bill credits free to low-income households.
Standard residential subscribers are guaranteed at least 20% savings on the value of bill credits; low-income subscribers get at least a 40% discount.
Income can be self-attested; early termination fees are banned under the consumer-protection frame.

Alternative On-Bill Credits are based on basic service rates (example cited: National Grid large ~10.79¢/kWh vs retail power often above 34¢). Independent developers; project size up to 5 MW, or 10 MW on brownfield/landfill sites.
drafts.body:
If you rent, or your roof is a no, the question is not "can I own panels."
It is "can I get a written discount on my bill."

Massachusetts SMART 3.0 is one of the clearest kitchen-table rulebooks in the country for community shared solar. New program-year design puts a big annual capacity frame on the board (about 900 megawatts). Shared projects have to serve lower-income households for real: either about 40% of the project is reserved for them, or at least 15% of bill credits go to them free. Everyday subscribers are supposed to see at least a 20% savings on the credit value. Low-income subscribers are supposed to see at least a 40% discount. Early termination fees are out. Income can be self-attested so people are not buried in paperwork.

Why the credit math matters: Alternative On-Bill Credits are tied to basic service, not the full retail sticker. One cited National Grid large basic-service figure sits near 10.79 cents per kilowatt-hour while retail power can run above 34 cents. That gap is where the household save lives, if the subscription contract is honest.

Sticky-note checklist for a 42-year-old renter in a walk-up, or a 60-year-old on a fixed income:

1) Ask for the written savings floor in percent of credit value, not a sales "up to."
2) Confirm you can leave without an early termination fee.
3) Ask whether income is self-attested and what documents they still want.
4) Compare the credit rate to your utility basic service, not a marketing average.
5) Soft-pedal battery add-ons unless you already want backup for outages.

35-54 line: Premium timelines save "written floor" checklists for renters, not slogans.

55+ line: a 20% or 40% discount only protects independence if the contract still works when you move or the project underperforms.

drafts.title: Solar for All court ruling: $7B program back on the board for bill cuts.
drafts.window: Friday 1 PM MT (pocketbook heat) or 8-9 PM surge for quieter read.
drafts.angle: Canary Media Sep 24, 2026: Rhode Island federal judge Mary S. McElroy ruled EPA's termination of Solar for All illegal. Program designed for more than $350M annual bill savings to more than 900,000 low-income and disadvantaged households over 5 years. Black Sun Light: ~1,000 Indiana households denied ≥20% bill cuts; Sunpath Solar scaled for 10,000 households on a $156M Georgia coalition grant; households paying $300-$400/mo utilities. Soft politics. Lead pocketbook and independence. EPA reviewing appeal = not money-in-hand yet.
bullets: Sep 24, 2026 Canary: Judge Mary S. McElroy (RI federal court) ruled EPA's Solar for All termination illegal.
Program design target: more than $350 million a year in bill savings for more than 900,000 low-income and disadvantaged households across a 5-year window.
Black Sun Light (Indiana): about 1,000 households that were lined up for at least 20% bill cuts were left hanging when funding froze.
Sunpath Solar had scaled toward about 10,000 households on a $156 million Georgia coalition grant path.
Many of the target households already pay $300-$400 a month for utilities. Soft-pedal politics; note EPA is reviewing appeal so cash is not in hands yet.
drafts.body:
This is not a victory lap.
It is a pocketbook story about households who cannot put panels on a roof.

A Rhode Island federal judge ruled that EPA's move to kill the Solar for All program was illegal. The program was designed to cut more than $350 million a year off bills for more than 900,000 low-income and disadvantaged households over about five years. In Indiana, Black Sun Light had about 1,000 households lined up for at least 20% bill cuts and then watched the freeze hit. In Georgia, Sunpath Solar had built toward about 10,000 households on a $156 million coalition grant path. A lot of these families already pay $300 to $400 a month just to keep the lights and heat on.

Kitchen-table sticky note for a 40-year-old renter, or a 58-year-old on a fixed income:

1) This ruling puts the program back on the board. It does not put a credit on your bill tomorrow.
2) Ask your state energy office or local nonprofit whether Solar for All money was already awarded in your county.
3) If you were on a waitlist for ≥20% bill cuts, call and ask whether your place in line is preserved.
4) Soft-pedal viral politics. Lead with "who gets the discount" and "when does cash flow."
5) Renters: community solar and income-qualified shared solar are still the doors that open without a roof.

35-54 line: Premium saves "bill cut for households without roofs," not culture-war threads.

55+ line: $300-$400 utility months are why independence math matters more than headlines.

drafts.title: UK Ofgem Oct-Dec 2026 price cap + Intelligent Octopus Go: shop the EV overnight rate.
drafts.window: Friday 4 PM MT or 8-11 PM surge (rate-shop read).
drafts.angle: Ofgem Oct 1-Dec 31 2026 price cap: electricity average 26.32p/kWh direct debit + 54.83p/day standing charge; VAT off electricity Oct 2026-Mar 2027. Intelligent Octopus Go smart-charges from about 8p/kWh (8.4p until Oct 1); up to about 69% less than average price-cap unit rate; typical save about £771 last year vs Flexible Octopus; 6 hours smart charging + 6 hours home off-peak 11:30pm-5:30am. Soft-pedal Wed UK Segen finance and Thu UK cloudy roof. US lesson: shop TOU / EV overnight rate before you buy the car.
bullets: Ofgem price cap (1 Oct-31 Dec 2026): average electricity unit rate about 26.32p/kWh on direct debit; standing charge about 54.83p/day.
Temporary VAT relief on electricity runs Oct 2026 through Mar 2027 (household bill context).
Intelligent Octopus Go: smart charging from about 8p/kWh (8.4p until 1 Oct); marketed as up to ~69% below the average price-cap unit rate.
Octopus cites typical savings around £771 last year versus Flexible Octopus for the right usage pattern.
Schedule frame: about 6 hours of smart charging plus 6 hours of home off-peak (11:30pm-5:30am).
drafts.body:
Do not buy the EV first and invent the charging plan later.

Britain just reset its retail electricity price cap for October through December 2026. Average unit rate on direct debit sits near 26.32 pence per kilowatt-hour, plus a standing charge near 54.83 pence per day. Against that backdrop, Intelligent Octopus Go is still the kitchen-table lesson: smart overnight charging from about 8 pence per kilowatt-hour, which the retailer pitches as up to about 69% below the average price-cap unit rate. Typical customers who fit the pattern saved about £771 last year versus a flexible default. The schedule is simple: about six hours of smart charging plus six hours of home off-peak from 11:30 at night to 5:30 in the morning.

US take for a 38-year-old shopping a first EV, or a 55-year-old who already owns one:

1) Call your utility and ask for the EV or overnight time-of-use rate before you sign a lease or loan.
2) Write the off-peak cents per kWh next to the public DC fast-charge price on your commute.
3) Confirm whether the cheap window is long enough for your real nightly miles.
4) Soft-pedal solar-loan APR stories and cloudy-roof geography today; this post is rate shopping.
5) Renters: ask whether the meter is in your name and whether an overnight EV rate can follow you.

35-54 line: Premium saves "shop the overnight rate before the car" posts.

55+ line: cheap overnight power only protects independence if you can actually plug in at home or work.

drafts.title: GM + PG&E Smart Charge Bundle: free home charger + $15/mo managed credits.
drafts.angle: Electrek Sep 23: GM "Smart Charge Bundle" with PG&E Charge Manager in Northern/Central California. Free GM PowerShift ($1,399-$1,999) OR PowerUp2 ($899) home charger on a new Chevy/Cadillac/GMC EV from a participating dealer with PG&E residential service. Buyer still pays install via Electrum partner. With OnStar: $15/mo bill credit for Charge Manager plus up to $50/mo more for shifting charge to optimal times. Runs until Feb 2027 or capacity. Managed charging = utility schedules when you charge (NOT bidirectional V2G). Soft-pedal CA 580 MW / Powerwall VPP LIVE. Lead free charger + monthly credit math. NOT a lease ladder.
bullets: Program: GM Smart Charge Bundle paired with PG&E Charge Manager for Northern and Central California residential customers.
Hardware: free GM PowerShift (about $1,399-$1,999 retail) or PowerUp2 (about $899); installation still on the buyer via Electrum partner.
Credits: $15 per month for Charge Manager participation with OnStar, plus up to $50 more per month based on how much charging shifts to optimal times.
Window: runs until February 2027 or until the program hits capacity; covers participating new Chevy, GMC, and Cadillac EVs.
Managed charging is one-way schedule control (utility picks when you charge). It is not V2G / send-power-back.
drafts.body:
A free charger is not free if the install quote and the monthly credits never show up on paper.

GM and PG&E are bundling a kitchen-table deal for Northern and Central California: buy a qualifying new Chevy, GMC, or Cadillac EV from a participating dealer on PG&E residential service, and you can get a free GM PowerShift or PowerUp2 home charger. Those boxes normally list around $899 to about $2,000. You still pay to install through GM's Electrum partner. Once you are on Charge Manager with OnStar, PG&E credits about $15 a month for participating, and you can earn up to about $50 more a month when more of your charging shifts to the hours the grid wants. The offer runs until February 2027 or until the seats fill up.

What managed charging actually means: the utility schedules when your car fills. You set how full you need to be and by when. You are not sending power back to the grid. That is a different product.

Sticky note for a 41-year-old GM shopper in the Bay Area or Central Valley, or a 57-year-old who wants the charger math without a battery sales pitch:

1) Ask the dealer in writing whether they are in the Smart Charge Bundle.
2) Get the Electrum install quote before you celebrate the "free" hardware.
3) Add $15/mo plus a realistic slice of the "up to $50" shift credit into your year-one total cost of ownership.
4) Confirm OnStar and Charge Manager enrollment steps on day one.
5) Soft-pedal home-battery VPP stories today; this post is charger + bill credit.

35-54 line: Premium saves "free charger + $15/mo" math, not lease payment ladders.

55+ line: a free wall box only helps independence if the install and the monthly credits are real on your bill.

drafts.title: Schneider Charge Pro Level 2: app-free QR charging for apartments and workplaces.
drafts.window: Friday 3 PM or 4 PM MT. Evening surge OK for renter audience.
drafts.angle: Jul 22 2026 PR: Schneider Electric Charge Pro for US commercial sites. QR scan to charge with no app and no account. Supports J1772 and NACS. Up to 80A (~19.2 kW). Aimed at multi-unit dwellings, workplaces, fleets, hotels, retail. One year EV Connect Software+ included; 5-year hardware warranty. Soft-pedal NYC curbside LIVE and Thu apt L2 $3.5k-$15k leftover twin. Different angle: ask landlord / employer for app-free NACS Level 2.
bullets: Schneider Charge Pro launched for the US commercial market (Jul 22 2026 PR).
Drivers can start a session with a QR scan; no app download and no account required for the basic flow.
Connector support: J1772 and NACS; power up to 80 amps (~19.2 kW Level 2).
Target sites: apartments / condos (MUDs), workplaces, fleets, hotels, retail.
Software: 1 year EV Connect Software+ included; hardware warranty 5 years.
drafts.body:
The charger at your apartment should not require a scavenger hunt for an app password.

Schneider Electric's Charge Pro is a commercial Level 2 box aimed at apartments, workplaces, fleets, hotels, and retail. Drivers can start with a QR scan. No app. No account for the basic path. It speaks both J1772 and NACS, so older plugs and Tesla-native cars are both in the conversation. Output goes up to about 80 amps, or roughly 19.2 kilowatts. Sites get a year of EV Connect Software+ and a five-year hardware warranty.

Kitchen-table ask for a 36-year-old renter, or a 59-year-old who parks at work five days a week:

1) Screenshot this and send it to your landlord or property manager: "Can we site an app-free NACS Level 2?"
2) Ask your employer the same question for the employee lot.
3) Soft-pedal "how much does a whole garage retrofit cost" today; start with one or two ports that people will actually use.
4) Confirm guest / visitor QR flow so family can charge without creating accounts.
5) Not NYC curbside. Not a battery. Just a wall box that does not fight you.

35-54 line: Premium saves "ask landlord for app-free NACS" posts.

55+ line: fewer apps means fewer barriers when you just want to plug in and go home.
